newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Malan sees Brazil growing with lower inflation.
newsitem.headline: Malan sees Brazil growing with lower inflation.

text.p: Brazil will not relax its hold on inflation in 1997, but the economy is still set for growth of between 4.5 and 5.0 percent, Finance Minister Pedro Malan said.
"Inflation under control and growth are completely compatible," Malan said during a recent meeting with foreign correspondents.

Brazilian gross domestic product was expected to grow by about six percent in the second half of 1996 after zero growth in the first six months, giving an average of three percent GDP growth for the year as a whole, Malan said.
"We are going to enter 1997 in a period of clear expansion," he said, predicting GDP growth of between 4.5 and 5.0 percent in the year as a whole and a similar performance in 1998.
"The economy has not gone into recession and it won't go into recession," Malan said, refering to recent speculation the government might cool down the economy to keep inflation at bay.
With inflation of about 10 percent in 1996, its lowest level since 1957, the government's focus in 1997 would be on narrowing the public sector budget deficit, the minsiter said.

Brazil's public sector operational deficit reached 3.98 percent in the first 11 months of the year, down from 5.0 percent in 1995 but way too high for the government to meet its target of a 2.5 percent deficit in 1996.

"The fiscal situation in 1996 was narrowly better than in 1995 although worse than our initial target ... and 1997 will be better than 1996," Malan said, adding that 1998 would show continuing improvement.

A program which encourages states and municipal governments to privatize, cut costs and raise more taxes in return for longer repayment terms for their debts with Brasilia would lead Brazil's fiscal improvement in 1997, Malan said.
States and municipalities reported an operational deficit of 2.18 percent in the January-November period, the biggest contribution to the overall 3.98 percent shortfall.
Pedro Parente, the Finance Ministry's executive secretary who drew up the program, said he expected the state and municipal share of the 1997 deficit to fall by about 40 percent.
Receipts from privatizations by state governments would come close to matching the $10 billion the federal government expects to raise from selloffs in 1997, Parente said.
At least $5.0 billion of the states' privatization receipts would be used to reduce their debts, he said.

So far nine states have agreed to join the federal government's program, including Sao Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul who account for more than 60 percent of roughly $50 billion in securitized debt owed by the states.
Six other states were close to reaching preliminary agreements to join the program, Parente said.
A virtual freeze on pay rises by federal, state and municipal governments in 1996 also pointed to a fiscal improvement in 1997, he said.
